units.evidence: [Wikipedia: James Ussher] lead: "the entrance of the night preceding the 23rd day of October ... the year before Christ 4004"; that is, around 6 pm on 22 October 4004 BC, per the proleptic Julian calendar. Same lead: "Archbishop of Armagh and Primate of All Ireland between 1625 and 1656". Body: "he calculated the date of the Creation to have been nightfall on 22 October 4004 BC".
units.note: The quote is verbatim (the ellipsis is in the source). 'Nightfall before 23 October' is the same as the source's nightfall on 22 October. He was archbishop when he published (1625 to 1656 covers 1650). The proleptic-Julian qualifier is left out, but the caption reports Ussher's own date, which is a fair simplification. The spoken line matches the caption ('Armah' is the right pronunciation of Armagh).

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: James Ussher]: "his most famous work, the Annales veteris testamenti, a prima mundi origine deducti ("Annals of the Old Testament, deduced from the first origins of the world"), which appeared in 1650 ... In this work, he calculated the date of the Creation to have been nightfall on 22 October 4004 BC."
units.note: The quote is verbatim. The source puts the Creation date in this work, so 'published the date in 1650' holds. The book is in Latin, and 'Annals of the Old Testament' is the source's own English rendering of the title. The spoken line matches.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: James Ussher]: "Ussher's account of historical events for which he had multiple sources other than the Bible is usually in close agreement with modern accounts – for example, he placed the death of Alexander in 323 BC and that of Julius Caesar in 44 BC."
units.note: The quote is verbatim. 'Several sources beyond the Bible' is 'multiple sources other than the Bible', 'usually hold up' is 'usually in close agreement with modern accounts', and the Caesar date is exact. The 'usually' qualifier is kept. The spoken line matches.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Age of Earth]: "The age of Earth is estimated to be 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years." ... "Estimates are based on radiometric dating of meteoritic material—the ages of which are approached by those of the oldest-known terrestrial material and lunar samples—and accretion models"
units.note: Both quotes are verbatim. 'About' covers the ±0.05. The caption does not mention meteorites or accretion models, but 'radiometric dating puts Earth's age at' is a true simplification. The spoken 'four point five four billion' matches.

units.evidence: [Commons File:Patricia_2015-10-23_1730Z.jpg]: "Hurricane Patricia shortly after peak intensity and approaching Western Mexico on October 23, 2015." The Commons page itself gives author "MODIS image captured by NASA’s Terra satellite", date 2015-10-23, location 18.3N 105.3W (offshore of Jalisco/Colima).
units.note: The quote is verbatim. 'Closes on the Pacific coast of Mexico' is a fair reading of 'approaching Western Mexico', and the Commons page confirms it is a satellite image. On voice only: the spoken line spells out the year ('twenty fifteen') but leaves the day as '23 October', while the other units spell it ('the twenty-third of October'). The meaning is the same, so this is a consistency nit, not a factual problem.
units.fix: Optional, voice only: spoken 'on the twenty-third of October, twenty fifteen'.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Hurricane Patricia]: "As Patricia neared its peak strength, the cyclone began to turn east-northeast towards Mexico." / "Late on October 23, dramatic weakening ensued and Patricia made landfall near Cuixmala, Jalisco, with winds of 150 mph (240 km/h)." Met. history: "In the five hours up until landfall in Mexico, Patricia weakened at an unprecedented rate while still over water." NHC TCR EP202015 (Kimberlain et al.): landfall "near Playa Cuixmala, around 2300 UTC 23 October with an intensity of 130 kt" (≈241 km/h).
units.note: Both quotes are verbatim. The order (turn near the peak, then fast weakening, then landfall at about 240 km/h) matches both the source and the NHC best track. The spoken respellings (Kweesh-mah-la, Ha-lees-ko) are reasonable and add no claims.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Hurricane Patricia] met. history: "Patricia dissipated on October 24 over central Mexico, less than 18 hours after moving ashore." Lead: "Within 24 hours of moving ashore, Patricia weakened into a tropical depression and dissipated soon thereafter". NHC TCR EP202015 best track: landfall 23/2300 UTC; tropical depression 24/1200 UTC; 'dissipated' 24/1800 UTC.
units.note: Second sentence: 'A day after landfall it was a depression', read literally, puts the storm at depression strength 24 hours after landfall. The pinned source's own meteorological history says it had dissipated 'less than 18 hours after moving ashore'. NHC's best track agrees: a depression about 13 h after landfall, gone by about 19 h. So at the one-day mark there was no storm left. Round 3's fix read 'Within a day of landfall'. The 'within' qualifier was dropped, and dropping it makes the sentence false. This needs fixing, not just polishing. First sentence: the record wording is now right. 'About a day and a half' checks out (hurricane strength 'shortly after 00:00 UTC on October 22' to peak 'around 12:00 UTC on October 23' is 36 h; NHC has 60 kt at 22/0000 to peak at 23/1200, also 36 h). But the sentence gives no starting point, and Patricia had been a tropical cyclone since 20 October (about 3.25 days to peak). Round 3's 'from a tropical storm' anchor was dropped as well.
units.fix: In about a day and a half Patricia grew from a tropical storm to the strongest sustained winds ever reliably measured or estimated in a tropical cyclone. Within a day of landfall it had weakened to a tropical depression.
units.resolved: Now "In about a day and a half Patricia went from tropical storm to the strongest sustained winds reliably measured or estimated in a tropical cyclone, and it faded within a day of landfall." (185 characters; "within" is back).

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Alberto Santos-Dumont] lead: "These were the first heavier-than-air flights certified by the Aeroclub of France, the first such flights officially witnessed by an aeronautics recordkeeping body, and the first of their kind recognised by the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale." Body: on 12 November he flew 220 m "winning the French Aeroclub Award".
units.note: All nine quotes are verbatim. The title carries the qualifier the claim depends on ('aeroplane' and 'an official body certified'), so it does not assert the Brazilian priority claim. It holds whichever flight counts: the body says the 23 October record 'was not made official', but the 12 November flight certainly was, and both were made by the 14-bis. On a 23 October card a viewer may assume the certified flight is that day's. Frame 4 settles it as 12 November, so this is acceptable.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Santos-Dumont 14-bis]: "was a pioneer era, canard-style biplane designed and built by Brazilian aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont". Commons description of m3: "Le 14-bis de Alberto Santos Dumont avec, en arrière-plan, le Blériot IV."
units.note: The quote is verbatim, and the image (m3) is the 14-bis, as its Commons description confirms. One caveat that leaves the claim true: the same article's body says he 'commissioned [Voisin] to help him construct' it and 'supervised construction', so 'built' means with Voisin's help. The spoken 'fourteen-bees' and 'Santos-Doomon' approximate the French pronunciation and add nothing.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Alberto Santos-Dumont]: "on 23 October 1906 flew about 60 metres at a height of two to three metres ... at the Bagatelle Gamefield in Paris, taking off unassisted by an external launch system." Body, 23 October section: "The plane lifted off and flew for 60 metres, without taking advantage of headwinds, ramps, catapults, slopes, or other devices."
units.note: Both quotes are verbatim, and the context confirms that the 'unaided' quote is about the 23 October flight (it sits under 'Oiseau de Proie II', 'On 23 October ...'). 'A few metres' covers both the 2 to 3 m here and the 14-bis article's 3 to 5 m. 'About 60 metres' also fits that article's 'over 50 metres'. Bagatelle is in the Bois de Boulogne, inside Paris. The spoken line matches.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Alberto Santos-Dumont] lead: "These were the first heavier-than-air flights certified by the Aeroclub of France ... and the first of their kind recognised by the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale." Body: 23 October "the record was not made official"; 12 November, 220 m "winning the French Aeroclub Award". Web: Wikipedia 'List of flight airspeed records' gives 12 Nov 1906, 41.292 km/h as the first officially recognised airspeed record; Universalis lists that day's first world records as duration 21 1/5 s, distance 220 m, speed 41.292 km/h.
units.note: The quotes are verbatim, and the narrowing to 12 November follows the article's body (23 October 'not made official'). A nit, not an error: the FAI recognised records from more than one flight that day. The 41.292 km/h speed record matches the earlier 82.60 m flight at 4:09 pm (the pinned body gives '41.3 km/h' for it), not the 220 m flight. So singular 'the 12 November flight ... first of its kind' slightly overcredits the 220 m flight. 'Of its kind' is loose enough to stay true (it was the first recognised distance and duration record). The source's own wording is plural. 'World body for air records' is a fair description of the FAI.
units.fix: Optional: France's Aero-Club certified the 12 November flights, and the world body for air records recognised them as the first of their kind.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Biplane]: "The first powered, controlled aeroplane to fly, the Wright Flyer, used a biplane wing arrangement". [Wikipedia: Alberto Santos-Dumont]: "These were the first heavier-than-air flights certified by the Aeroclub of France ... and the first of their kind recognised by the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale."
units.note: Both quotes are verbatim. 'The first one' takes its noun from the previous sentence ('powered, controlled aeroplane'), so round 3's missing 'aeroplane' qualifier is now there and the sentence no longer covers balloon or airship certifications. The wording is clunky: 'made the first one a record body certified' can be misheard, especially in the voice line ('Santos-Doomon made the first one a record body certified'), as Santos-Dumont making the first one, full stop. Adding 'that' removes the garden path. The spoken line otherwise matches the caption.
units.fix: Optional, for clarity: The first powered, controlled aeroplane to fly was the Wright brothers' Flyer. Santos-Dumont made the first one that a record body certified.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Biplane]: "The first powered, controlled aeroplane to fly, the Wright Flyer"; [Wikipedia: Alberto Santos-Dumont]: "These were the first heavier-than-air flights certified by the Aeroclub of France, the first such flights officially witnessed by an aeronautics recordkeeping body".
units.note: All quotes are verbatim. 'The Wright Flyer flew first' (1903 against 1906) and 'the first aeroplane flight that an official body certified' are both supported, and the second holds whether the certified flight is 23 October or 12 November. I know of no earlier certified heavier-than-air flight: the 13 September 1906 hop was watched by Aéro-Club observers but 'did not qualify for any prize' (14-bis article), and the Vuia and Ellehammer hops of 1906 were not certified by a record body.

units.evidence: Image viewed (1890×1092 original): a fish-like animal with its front half and leg-like pectoral fin on a pale sandy shore and its tail in shallow water, with reeds behind. Commons: 'Life restoration of Tiktaalik roseae, a transitional fossil ... between sarcopterygian fishes and tetrapods'; author 'Zina Deretsky, National Science Foundation'; {{PD-USGov-NSF}}; 1890×1092. The NSF source the Commons page cites (news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=106807) is Press Release 06-055 of April 5, 2006 (Wayback snapshot 2006-04-18). It carries the same illustration (tiktaalik_f.jpg, which I viewed) captioned 'Fossil fish bridges evolutionary gap between animals of land and sea', the title in Commons' 'other fields'.
units.note: The alt matches the picture, and 'early fish' is fair for a sarcopterygian of 375 million years ago. The licence and size match media.json and Commons. The 2006 in the credit is right: Commons' date field (2009-07-09) is only the Flickr upload, and NSF published the illustration on 5 April 2006.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Black Death in England]: "which reached England in June 1348"; "a figure of 40–60% of the population is widely accepted"; "The most immediate consequence was a halt to the campaigns of the Hundred Years' War."
units.note: All quotes are verbatim, and the 40 to 60% figure is about England's population, which matches 'the people'. Historical nuance, not an error against the pinned source: the Truce of Calais (September 1347) had already paused fighting before the plague arrived, and the plague kept the truce going rather than starting it. The source's wording ('a halt to the campaigns') supports 'halts'. The spoken line matches.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Black Death in England]: "A study reported in 2011 of skeletons exhumed from the Black Death cemetery in East Smithfield, London, found Yersinia pestis DNA." / "caused by Yersinia pestis bacteria".
units.note: Both quotes are verbatim. 'That cemetery' refers to East Smithfield, named in frame 3. Independent check: the East Smithfield Y. pestis DNA papers were published in 2011 (Schuenemann et al., PNAS, and Bos et al., Nature). The spoken 'twenty eleven' matches.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Auld Alliance]: "In October 1295, a Scottish embassy to France agreed to the Treaty of Paris, which was signed on 23 October." Lead: "an alliance between the kingdoms of Scotland and France against England made in 1295". Web: breakingofbritain.ac.uk ('This week: 22-23 October 1295' and '23 February 1296'): treaty concluded at Paris on 23 October 1295 and ratified by King John at Dunfermline on 23 February 1296.
units.note: The quote is verbatim. The lead's 'signed by John Balliol and Philip IV' can look like a conflict with 'Scottish envoys sign', but it is not: on 23 October the envoys concluded the treaty in the king's name, and Balliol ratified it in February 1296. 'Paris' rests on the treaty's name and on independent sources. The spoken line matches.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Auld Alliance]: "In the short term, however, the treaty proved to be no protection against Edward, whose swift and devastating invasion of Scotland in 1296 all but eradicated its independence."
units.note: The quote is verbatim. 'Did not protect' is 'no protection', and 'nearly ended' is 'all but eradicated'. The spoken 'Edward the First' matches.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Auld Alliance]: "The alliance was renewed by all the French and Scottish monarchs of that period except Louis XI." / "In 1558, the alliance between the two kingdoms was revived with the marriage of Mary, Queen of Scots to the future Francis II of France". Body also notes renewals in 1326 and reviews in 1512, 1517 and 1548.
units.note: Both quotes are verbatim. 'Renewed for centuries' (1295 to 1558) is supported, and the 1558 marriage is exact. The spoken line matches.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Survival of the fittest]: "Herbert Spencer first used the phrase, after reading Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species, in his Principles of Biology (1864)".
units.note: The quote is verbatim, and the attribution and year are exact. 'Sounds like Darwin' is framing, not a claim. The spoken line drops the quotation marks, which the voice cannot say anyway, and the meaning is unchanged.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Survival of the fittest]: "In July 1866, Alfred Russel Wallace wrote to Darwin about readers thinking that the phrase "natural selection" personified nature as "selecting" and said this misconception could be avoided "by adopting Spencer's term"".
units.note: The quote is verbatim, and the July 1866 date and the 'worry' (the personification misreading) match. 'How do we know Darwin borrowed it? His letters.' holds: Darwin's reply calls it 'H. Spencer's excellent expression'. The source also gives printed evidence (Variation, 1868, and the Origin's fifth edition 'gave full credit to Spencer'), so the letters are one good answer, not the only one. The spoken line matches.

units.evidence: [Wikipedia: Survival of the fittest]: "I fully agree with all that you say on the advantages of H. Spencer's excellent expression of 'the survival of the fittest'. This however had not occurred to me till reading your letter." / "In On the Origin of Species, he introduced the phrase in the fifth edition published in 1869".
units.note: Both quotes are verbatim, and the paraphrase ('the advantages ... had not occurred to him until he read the letter') is faithful. The caption does not claim the Origin was his first printed use, which is correct to avoid: the source says he first 'adopted the phrase in The Variation of Animals and Plants Under Domestication published in 1868'. The spoken line matches.
